ideas.title: Theme Conflict Merge
ideas.summary: For small Shopify merchants whose theme update failed with 'code edits could not be included': upload the old and new theme, get back a merged copy with your edits carried over file by file and a plain-language list of the few places that need a decision.

public.summary: When a theme update refuses to keep your custom changes, this carries them over for you and shows you only the few spots that need a decision.
public.problem: You paid someone to tweak your store's theme, and now the theme has an update with fixes you want. You click update and get a message that your code edits could not be included, so the new version arrives without any of your changes. Your choices are to stay on the old version, hire a developer to copy everything across by hand, or hope you remember what was changed.
public.forWhom: Shop owners on Shopify who have edited their theme, or had someone edit it for them, and want to keep getting theme updates.
benefits: Keep your custom changes when you update your theme
Know exactly which changes need a human decision, in plain words
Stop paying a developer every time the theme updates
See the updated store side by side with the old one before anything goes live
Your live store stays untouched until you choose to switch

ideas.problemStatement: I tried to update my theme and Shopify said a copy was added but my code edits could not be included because 'Rebase failed with conflicts' on ten files. I don't know which of my changes are missing, and copying old files over the new version breaks the update itself.
ideas.description: The merchant downloads two theme ZIPs from the Shopify admin (the live, customized theme and the new version Shopify added to the library) and uploads them. The tool finds the stock version the store was originally installed from (public release tags for Horizon and Dawn on GitHub; other themes need the merchant's original ZIP) and runs a three-way merge file by file, so that one conflict no longer throws away every edit, which is what Shopify's built-in updater does today. Non-conflicting customizations are applied automatically; each real conflict is shown as a short plain-language card ('you changed the cart button text here; the update also changed this button') with a choose-mine, choose-theirs, or ask-a-developer option. Store-specific files (settings_data.json, locales, JSON templates) are labeled as settings, not code, so they do not drown the list. The output is a merged ZIP the merchant uploads as an unpublished theme, plus side-by-side screenshots of the home, product and cart pages for a visual check.
ideas.targetCustomer: Owners of small Shopify stores (one to ten staff) on Horizon or Dawn who have edited theme code themselves, with Sidekick, or through a past freelancer, and whose theme update reported that code edits could not be included.
ideas.buyer: The store owner, on the business card, from the same budget that pays for apps and occasional freelance theme work (one freelancer.com job for this task offered $30 to $250).
ideas.whyNow: Horizon, Shopify's newest free theme, ships updates every few weeks (3.3.1 to 3.5.1 to 4.14 to 4.15 in 2026), and Shopify's own updater drops all code edits when any file conflicts. Shopify staff said in August 2025 they were working on it, and the thread was still open in September 2026. The paid updater with 291 reviews (OOTS) does not list Horizon among the themes it supports.
ideas.founderFit: Three-way merge is version control, which Pisan teaches, and the core is a deterministic diff3 over text files that he can build and test alone with real theme release tags. It needs no paid API at runtime and no access to the merchant's store in the first version, because it works on downloaded ZIPs.

problemEvidence.summary: A paying Theme Updater subscriber says updates delete their theme customizations and they had to pay a developer $300 extra; the app has 291 reviews and charges $9/month.

competitors.name: Shopify built-in theme update
competitors.gap: Carries code edits over only when nothing conflicts; one conflicting file means none of the edits are included.

competitors.name: Theme Updater & Backups (Out of the Sandbox)
competitors.price: Free plan; Updater Pro $9/month or $96/year; 4.2 from 291 reviews
competitors.gap: Lists Dawn and partner themes but not Horizon; 1 and 2 star reviews say customizations are still lost.

competitors.name: Theme Drift: Compare & Diff
competitors.gap: Shows three-way conflicts but leaves the merge to the merchant or to a paid migration service.

competitors.name: DiffMate
competitors.gap: Diff editor that copies changes between themes one by one; no automatic merge.

competitors.name: Theme Ledger
competitors.gap: Read-only plain-English report of custom code; Dawn only; does not produce a merged theme.

competitors.name: ThemeWatch
competitors.gap: Two-theme comparison only; read-only.

competitors.name: Diffy Theme Tools
competitors.gap: Diff, backups and history; no merge.

keyFeatures: Three-way merge per file against the stock release the store started from
Automatic carry-over of non-conflicting edits, so one conflict no longer drops everything
Plain-language conflict cards with mine / theirs / ask-a-developer choices
Settings files labeled as settings, not code
Side-by-side screenshots of home, product and cart pages
A developer hand-off note listing only the unresolved conflicts

features: Upload two theme ZIPs; Horizon and Dawn base versions fetched from public GitHub tags
diff3 merge per file with conflict cards
Merged ZIP download for upload as an unpublished theme
outOfScope: Writing to the store through the Admin API (needs Shopify's protected Asset access scope)
Third-party paid themes without a merchant-supplied original ZIP

ideas.techStack: React + Vite, a browser-side diff3 library (no upload of theme code to a server in the free check), Supabase for accounts and payments, Playwright for screenshots in a later version.

pricing.model: Per update, with a cheap subscription for frequent Horizon updaters
pricing.rationale: Sits between Theme Drift's $19.99 one-time compare and the $30 to $250 a merchant offers a freelancer for the same job; under OOTS's $9/month.

ideas.revenueSketch: Estimate: 150 merchants a month at $19 = $2,850/month, assuming a 2 to 3 percent conversion from free conflict checks driven by forum answers. Unvalidated.
ideas.distribution: Answer the recurring 'code edits could not be included' and 'rebase failed with conflicts' threads on community.shopify.com with a free conflict check; list on the Shopify App Store only after the ZIP version proves demand.

validationTest.method: Ship the free browser-only check (upload two ZIPs, see how many edits would carry over and how many conflict) and offer the merged ZIP for $19 to merchants found in forum threads.
validationTest.successCriteria: Out of 40 free checks, 8 or more paid merges, and at least 5 merchants who report the merged theme went live without a developer.
validationTest.cost: About 2 weeks of evenings and $0 beyond hosting.

ideas.moat: Weak. The merge itself is standard; the defensible part would be a library of per-theme base versions and file-type rules (JSON templates, settings, locales) tuned on real merges. Shopify could fix its updater at any time.
compliance: Shopify app review: writing assets back to a theme from a public app needs Shopify's protected Asset access scope, so the first version works on downloaded ZIPs and never writes to the store.
Privacy: theme code can contain API keys or tracking IDs; the free check runs in the browser and nothing is stored.
Licensing: paid themes' code is licensed to the merchant; the tool must not keep or redistribute base versions of paid themes.

risks.risk: Shopify ships a better merge in its built-in updater (staff said they were working on it).
risks.mitigation: Keep the build small and ZIP-based; pivot the conflict cards into a developer hand-off tool if Shopify closes the gap.

risks.risk: Liquid and JSON merges that are textually clean but break the store.
risks.mitigation: Always output an unpublished theme, show page screenshots, and never publish.

risks.risk: Crowded category: seven theme diff and update apps, four launched in 2026.
risks.mitigation: Compete on the one thing none of them does for Horizon: produce a merged theme, not a diff.

scoreRationale.pain: Four independent merchants in 2026 hit failed or damaging theme updates: https://community.shopify.com/t/update-theme-error-rebase-failed-with-conflicts/630057 and https://community.shopify.com/t/i-have-a-problem-with-my-store/675548
scoreRationale.willingnessToPay: One dated paid job ($30 to $250, https://www.freelancer.com/projects/git/Shopify-Theme-Update-Diff-Migrate) and a $9/month app with 291 reviews (https://apps.shopify.com/theme-updater-by-out-of-the-sandbox); reviewer: people pay to have it done, not much for software.
scoreRationale.reachability: Self-serve via forum answers, but the App Store category is crowded with 7+ theme diff/update apps (https://apps.shopify.com/theme-change-monitor).
scoreRationale.competitiveGap: Shopify's free updater already merges non-conflicting edits (https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-store/themes/managing-themes/updating-themes); Theme Drift sells a 3-way compare for $19.99.
scoreRationale.feasibility: A correct merge across Liquid, JSON templates, settings and locales is harder than it looks, as the Theme Drift feedback thread notes: https://community.shopify.com/t/looking-for-merchants-agencies-who-struggle-when-a-customized-theme-gets-an-update-feedback-on-theme-drift-2-3-way-theme-compare/686301
scoreRationale.complianceBurden: Writing a merged theme from a public app needs Shopify's protected Asset access scope (https://shopify.dev/docs/api/admin-rest/latest/resources/asset), which is why the first version works on ZIPs.

review.findings: Adversarial reviewer recommended a kill and rescored from 23 to 17: competitiveGap 2->1 because Shopify's free updater already carries over non-conflicting edits and Theme Drift ($19.99 one-time 3-way compare), DiffMate (free) and Theme Upgrade Buddy (free) cover the compare-and-copy step; WTP 4->3 because the paid evidence is one $30-250 freelancer job and a $9/month app; reachability 4->3 (7+ apps in the category); feasibility 4->3 (Liquid/JSON/settings merge is hard); compliance 5->3 (theme asset writes need a protected scope). The reviewer also identified the one remaining wedge: Shopify's updater is all or nothing, so a single conflict drops every edit, and OOTS does not list Horizon. The idea was re-scoped to exactly that case, working on downloaded ZIPs to avoid the protected scope, and ships as provisional at the reviewer's 17 because it is the only candidate today that survived review with a residual gap; the other five reviewed candidates were killed outright.

missing: competitiveGap 1: Shopify's free updater and several cheap diff apps cover most of the job
gateGap.closedBy: The validation test's paid merges close the largest gap: 8 paid $19 merges out of 40 free checks would show that merchants pay for a merged theme rather than a diff, which would justify raising competitiveGap to 2 and willingnessToPay to 4. Reaching 22 also needs reachability 4, shown by forum answers converting without App Store listing.

ideas.title: Accessibility Fleet Log
ideas.summary: For web agencies and freelancers who look after 10 to 100 small-business WordPress sites: one dashboard showing every client site's accessibility status, a dated statement and issue log per site, and white-label client reports, built on free checkers that run on the client's own server.

public.summary: See the accessibility status of every client website you look after in one place, with a dated record and a clean report you can send each client.
public.problem: You look after dozens of client websites, and each one needs an accessibility check, a statement, and some proof that you are keeping on top of it. The plugin you used to rely on now pushes upsells and its own branding onto your clients' dashboards, and sends visitor data to someone else's servers. The tools that do this well for many sites at once are priced for big companies.
public.forWhom: Web agencies and freelancers who maintain WordPress sites for small businesses.
benefits: Every client site's accessibility status on one screen
A dated record of issues and fixes for each site
Reports with your own name on them, ready to send
Nothing extra on your clients' dashboards
Visitor data stays on each client's own site

ideas.problemStatement: I manage multiple client websites and the accessibility plugin I put on all of them turned into upsell adware with 'powered by' branding and dashboard widgets; I had to write PHP snippets to hide it and finally uninstalled it across my whole fleet. In the EU it also loads Google Analytics from the vendor's CDN, so I cannot use it for GDPR clients.
ideas.description: A small companion plugin is installed on each client site. It reads results from free engines that already run on the site itself (Equalize Digital Accessibility Checker free, Editoria11y, Sa11y) and sends only issue counts, rule IDs and page URLs (no visitor data) to the agency's dashboard. The dashboard lists every site with open issues by WCAG criterion, the date each was found and fixed, and a dated accessibility statement (EAA/BFSG and ADA wording) per site. Each month it produces a white-label PDF report per client. It is not an overlay and claims no compliance; it records what was checked and when.
ideas.targetCustomer: Web agencies and freelance WordPress developers who maintain 10 to 100 separate (non-multisite) client sites for small businesses, many with EU clients.
ideas.buyer: The agency owner, from the care-plan margin they already charge clients for maintenance; the same budget that pays for ManageWP/MainWP and plugin licences.
ideas.whyNow: Elementor took over the widely installed One Click Accessibility plugin and rebranded it as Ally, and its 2026 one-star reviews are agencies and EU users leaving over upsells, branding and a CDN that loads Google Analytics. The European Accessibility Act has applied since 2025-06-28, so EU clients now ask for statements. The incumbent with a network view (Equalize Digital) sells it only in its $2,250/year 25-site Agency plan, and only for WordPress multisite.
ideas.founderFit: Pisan works in accessibility and can ship a WordPress plugin plus a Supabase dashboard alone. The product reuses free open-source checkers rather than building a new rules engine, and needs no paid API at runtime.

ideas.techStack: WordPress plugin (PHP), React + Vite + Tailwind dashboard, Supabase (auth, Postgres), server-side PDF generation

pricing.rationale: Undercuts Equalize Digital's $2,250/yr 25-site Agency plan (about $188/month) while relying on its free engine; agencies bill accessibility into care plans, so the cost is passed through.

ideas.revenueSketch: Estimate: 60 agencies x $40/month average = $2,400 MRR. Assumes agencies leaving Ally convert at a low single-digit rate from wordpress.org and agency communities.
ideas.distribution: A free listing in the WordPress plugin directory for the companion plugin; replies in the Ally and Equalize support forums where agencies ask for fleet features; WordPress agency communities and meetups; WP care-plan newsletters.

validationTest.method: Publish a landing page with a clickable mock of the fleet dashboard and a sample white-label report, and show it to 10 agencies that maintain 10 or more client sites, reached through WordPress agency communities and the plugin forums.

Liability: clients may treat a statement as proof of compliance; disclaimers and wording reviewed once by a lawyer.

risks.risk: Equalize Digital adds a cheap non-multisite agency dashboard.
risks.mitigation: Support several free engines, not only Equalize, and compete on white-label reporting and price.

risks.risk: The pain is anger at one vendor, not demand for a new tool.

risks.risk: Checking rendered pages needs a browser, and free engines run in the editor or front end.
risks.mitigation: Report what the on-site engines find; leave scheduled headless scans out of the MVP.

scoreRationale.pain: Real, recent agency and EU complaints, but they are about one plugin's upsells and CDN, not a missing fleet tool: https://wordpress.org/support/topic/unusable-bloatware-replaced-on-every-site-i-manage/
scoreRationale.willingnessToPay: Agencies already pay Equalize up to $2,250/yr and buy Ally licences: https://equalizedigital.com/accessibility-checker/pricing/ and https://wordpress.org/support/topic/plugin-has-no-valid-header-8/
scoreRationale.reachability: Unhappy agencies are visible in plugin reviews, but only one or two agency voices so far: https://wordpress.org/support/plugin/pojo-accessibility/reviews/?filter=1
scoreRationale.competitiveGap: Equalize already does on-server checks, a statement generator and multisite; the gap is a cheap fleet view for separate installs: https://wordpress.org/plugins/accessibility-checker/
scoreRationale.feasibility: Rendered-page checks need a browser; free engines run in-browser, so the MVP depends on their output: https://wordpress.org/plugins/editoria11y-accessibility-checker/
scoreRationale.complianceBurden: No visitor data leaves the site, but statements for EAA/ADA invite reliance as proof of compliance: https://wordpress.org/plugins/accessibility-checker/

review.findings: The reviewer confirmed the five Ally reviews (2025-07 to 2026-11, different authors) but found they target Elementor's widget, upsells and CDN, not a missing checker, and the Northwoods agency had already moved to a free alternative. Equalize Digital's free plugin already checks WCAG on the server, generates a statement and needs no external API, so a new checker would fail; the idea was re-scoped to a fleet layer over free engines (aggregated status, dated log and statement archive, white-label reports), the one gap left because Equalize's network view needs multisite and the $2,250/yr Agency plan. Scores: pain 3, WTP 4, reachability 3, competitiveGap 2, feasibility 3, complianceBurden 3.

missing: pain 3 is below 4: the complaints are about one vendor's plugin, not about lacking a fleet view
no agency has yet asked for a cross-site accessibility dashboard in its own words
gateGap.closedBy: The validation test's 10 agency demos close the largest gap (pain and the missing direct ask): if 3 of 10 pay a first month, pain rises to 4 and the evidence includes direct requests, which would lift the total to about 21 to 22.

ideas.title: Health Page Tracker Watch
ideas.summary: For therapists, med spas, wellness studios and small clinics: a monthly scan of the booking and service pages that lists every third-party script and widget that sends visitors' page addresses and IPs to a vendor, flags which of those vendors will not sign a BAA or fall under consumer-health-data laws, and alerts when a new one appears.

public.summary: Know which outside tools on your booking and service pages are sending visitor information to other companies, and hear about it when a new one shows up.
public.problem: Your website was put together with a booking widget, a chat box, an accessibility tool and an analytics tag, and each one quietly sends the address of the page a visitor is reading to its maker. On a page about therapy, fertility or weight loss, that can count as health information. You rarely know which tools are on the site, and a plugin update can add a new one without telling you.
public.forWhom: Owners of small health and wellness practices and the people who run their websites.
benefits: A plain list of every outside tool on your health pages
Know which vendors will and will not sign a privacy agreement
An alert when an update adds a new tracker
A dated report to keep with your privacy records
A short list of fixes your web person can act on

ideas.problemStatement: I build sites for health practices and need to know whether the accessibility plugin sends anything from health-intent pages to its servers and whether the vendor will sign a BAA; the vendor confirmed it sends the page URL, IP and device data and offered only a GDPR DPA.
ideas.description: The owner or their web person enters the site; a headless browser visits the booking, intake and service pages, records every third-party request, and matches each host against a maintained vendor table (does the vendor sign a BAA, what it receives, whether a consumer-health-data law such as Washington's My Health My Data Act is likely in scope). The report lists each tool by page in plain words with a suggested fix (remove, switch to a vendor that signs, move off health-intent pages). A monthly rescan alerts only on changes. The vendor table, kept current by hand from vendor terms, is the product; the scan itself is commodity.
ideas.targetCustomer: Small health and wellness businesses (solo therapists, group practices, med spas, wellness studios, small dental and physical-therapy offices) and the freelancers or agencies who run their websites.
ideas.buyer: The practice owner on the business card, or a web agency that resells it in a care plan.
ideas.whyNow: Widget vendors keep adding CDN-loaded scripts (Elementor's Ally confirmed in October 2026 that it sends URL, IP and device data and offered no BAA). Although HHS's tracking-technology guidance was vacated in 2024, private class actions over pixels on provider booking pages continue (the Aspen Dental settlement), and Washington's My Health My Data Act covers wellness businesses that HIPAA does not.
ideas.founderFit: Pisan can build a Playwright crawler and a Supabase dashboard alone, and his interest in AI ethics and accessibility fits a privacy audit; it needs no paid API at runtime.

problemEvidence.author: webmastercreativeklick
problemEvidence.summary: A site builder for health clients asks whether Ally sends data from health-intent pages and whether Elementor signs a BAA; Elementor confirmed URL, IP and device data are sent and offered only a GDPR DPA; unresolved.

problemEvidence.summary: The accessibility plugin loads Google Analytics hidden in a CDN script, discovered just before go-live (GDPR, not health-specific).

competitors.gap: Nearly the same product at $39; no sign of a maintained BAA table for accessibility, chat and booking widgets, and pricing is still draft.

keyFeatures: Crawl of booking, intake and service pages with every third-party request recorded
Maintained vendor table: BAA available or not, data received, consumer-health-data law exposure
Plain-language report by page with a suggested fix
Monthly rescan that alerts only on new or changed trackers

features: Single-site scan of up to 20 pages
Vendor table for the 50 most common widgets and pixels
Report and monthly change alert by email

ideas.techStack: Playwright on a small server, React + Vite + Tailwind, Supabase (auth, Postgres, scheduled jobs), email via a transactional provider

pricing.pricePoint: $19/month per site; agency bundle of 10 sites at $99/month
pricing.rationale: Below Sift Health's $39 and Patient Protect's $39 platform; the free one-off scanners set the floor, so the paid part is monitoring and the vendor table.

ideas.revenueSketch: Estimate: 120 sites x $19/month = $2,280 MRR, assuming most sales come through web agencies serving health practices.
ideas.distribution: Agencies that build therapist and med-spa sites (reached through the WordPress support threads where they ask about BAAs), therapy-practice technology communities such as PersonCenteredTech's audience, and a free one-page scan as the entry point.

validationTest.method: Run the free scan by hand on 30 public therapist, med-spa and wellness-studio booking pages, email each owner or listed web agency their own findings, and offer monthly monitoring at $19.
validationTest.successCriteria: 5 of 30 reply asking what to fix, and 3 pay for the first month.

ideas.moat: The hand-maintained vendor table (which widgets sign BAAs and what each sends) and the history of changes per site.
compliance: HIPAA / MHMDA: the product must not give legal opinions; it reports what is sent and what vendors' own terms say, with a disclaimer.
Legal context: HHS's 2022 tracking guidance was vacated in 2024 (AHA v. Becerra), so whether an IP plus a public-page visit is PHI is disputed; copy must say so.
Data: the scan reads public pages only and stores no patient data.

risks.risk: Sift Health already sells the same monitoring at $39 for the same buyer.
risks.mitigation: Compete on price and on the widget vendor table; if Sift drops to $19 or adds the table, stop.

risks.risk: After the 2024 vacatur, small practices feel less urgency.
risks.mitigation: Lead with the wellness businesses HIPAA does not cover but MHMDA does, and with class-action exposure.

risks.risk: 'This vendor will not sign a BAA, remove it' reads as legal advice.
risks.mitigation: Report vendor terms as facts with links, never conclusions; have a lawyer review wording once.

scoreRationale.pain: One unresolved recent complaint from a builder for health clients, and the rest is vendor content: https://wordpress.org/support/topic/elementor-ally-data-handling-baa-confirmation/
scoreRationale.willingnessToPay: Independent practices pay $39 per office per month for a platform that includes this: https://patient-protect.com/pricing
scoreRationale.reachability: Practices are fragmented; the route is through web agencies and therapy-tech communities: https://personcenteredtech.com/tag/google-analytics/
scoreRationale.competitiveGap: Free scanners exist and Sift Health offers $39 monitoring: https://hipaa-scan.echo-factory.com/ and https://sift-health.pages.dev/pricing/
scoreRationale.feasibility: Crawling and classifying requests is routine; keeping the vendor table current is the ongoing work: https://wordpress.org/support/topic/elementor-ally-data-handling-baa-confirmation/
scoreRationale.complianceBurden: Findings border on legal advice and the PHI question is disputed after the vacatur: https://www.quarles.com/newsroom/publications/hhs-ocr-withdraws-tracking-technologies-appeal-in-aha-v-becerra

review.findings: The reviewer found the one-off scan is free from several vendors (Echo-Factory, Patient Protect, Captain Compliance) and Sift Health already offers $39/month monitoring with weekly rescans for this buyer, so the idea was re-scoped to a cheaper monitor whose value is a maintained table of which widget vendors (accessibility, chat, booking) sign BAAs, plus MHMDA scoping for wellness businesses HIPAA does not cover. Urgency is weaker since HHS withdrew its appeal in AHA v. Becerra; the live risk is private class actions (the Aspen Dental settlement involved a large dental chain, not a small practice), and no MHMDA suit against a small practice was found. ideas.title: Client Safe-Edit Pack for n8n
ideas.summary: For freelancers who build n8n automations for small-business clients: upload the workflow export, tick the values the client may change (prompts, business rules, recipients), and get back an importable form-and-config add-on so the client edits only those, plus a run-it-yourself acceptance test that proves the workflow still works.

public.summary: Let your clients safely change the few settings they care about in the automations you built, without touching anything that could break them.
public.problem: You build an automation for a client, and they want to tweak a prompt or change who gets the weekly email. Giving them the full editor means they can break everything, and the proper permission controls cost far more than a small client will pay. So you get the call every time a word needs changing, or the call three months later when something they changed stopped working.
public.forWhom: Freelancers and small agencies who build automations for small-business clients.
benefits: Clients change prompts and settings on their own
The rest of the automation stays out of reach
A simple test the client can run to see it still works
Fewer 'it stopped working' calls
A cleaner handover you can charge for

ideas.problemStatement: I want an easy way for my clients to update the AI nodes themselves without getting lost in everything; is there a permission where they can only update the parts I document? When I hand over, the client doesn't know what they can safely change, and three months later I get the 'it stopped working' call.
ideas.description: The freelancer uploads an exported workflow JSON. The app lists every Set node, prompt field and literal value, and the freelancer ticks the ones the client may change and gives each a plain label. It generates two importable files: a small n8n add-on (an n8n Form Trigger plus a Data Table that holds those values, with the original nodes rewired to read from it) so the client edits values through a form instead of the editor, and an acceptance-test workflow with a sample input, the expected output and one failure case to replay. Everything runs in the browser on the export; the app never holds the client's n8n credentials or API key.
ideas.targetCustomer: Freelancers and small agencies who build n8n automations for small-business clients on n8n Cloud Starter or self-hosted Community edition, where real per-role restrictions are not available.
ideas.buyer: The freelancer, on their own card, priced per client handover so they can pass it through on the invoice.
ideas.whyNow: n8n's restrictive roles sit behind Cloud Pro (Project Editor) and Enterprise (Viewer and custom roles), while n8n added Data Tables that can hold configuration. In October 2026 the n8n forum had several threads on client handover, and at least three indie handover and audit products launched there, none offering a client-safe edit surface.
ideas.founderFit: The core is a deterministic transform of workflow JSON, a version-control and testing problem Pisan teaches; it is a browser-only React app he can ship in a weekend, with no paid API and no stored secrets.

ideas.techStack: React + Vite + Tailwind, browser-only JSON transforms, Stripe Checkout for per-handover payment, static hosting

pricing.model: Per client handover, with an optional builder plan
pricing.rationale: Every confirmed price in this niche is one-off ($9 to $19), so per-handover pricing matches how builders already pay, and they can bill it to the client.

ideas.revenueSketch: Estimate: 150 packs/month x $15 = $2,250/month, assuming 50 to 100 active n8n freelancers using it a few times a month.
ideas.distribution: The n8n community forum, where handover threads appear weekly and product posts are tolerated; n8n template creators; freelancers who post fixed-price n8n services.

validationTest.method: Build a by-hand version for 5 freelancers who posted in the October 2026 handover threads: take one real workflow export each and return the form add-on and acceptance test, then offer the next one at $15.
validationTest.successCriteria: 3 of 5 deploy it with a client and 2 pay for a second pack.

ideas.moat: Thin: correct rewiring across n8n versions and node types is fiddly, and a library of tested patterns (AI agent prompts, email recipients, schedules) builds up with use.
compliance: Secrets: workflow exports can contain secrets in node parameters; process exports only in the browser and say so.
No client data or n8n API keys are stored.
Accessibility: the generated client form uses n8n's own form pages; the app's own UI needs WCAG 2.2 AA.

risks.risk: n8n ships cheaper per-field permissions or client forms.
risks.mitigation: Keep the build to two weekends so a native feature costs little; pivot the transform to Make if it happens.
The validation test asks for payment on the second pack before more is built.

risks.risk: Rewiring breaks on unusual node types.
risks.mitigation: Support only Set nodes, AI prompt fields and email recipients at first, and generate the acceptance test to catch breakage.

scoreRationale.pain: One clearly independent buyer voice; the other threads come from builders validating their own products: https://community.n8n.io/t/best-examples-of-documenting-an-n8n-workflow-to-leave-with-non-technical-clients/325506
scoreRationale.willingnessToPay: Only one-off $9 to $19 prices are confirmed, and no one is shown paying for client-safe editing: https://n8n-handoff-kit.vercel.app/how-to-document-n8n-workflows-for-clients.html
scoreRationale.reachability: The n8n forum is full of these builders and tolerates product posts: https://community.n8n.io/t/how-do-you-hand-over-n8n-workflows-to-clients-heres-the-format-im-working-on/322030
scoreRationale.competitiveGap: Static handover docs and a free client portal exist; only the safe-edit form and acceptance test are open: https://railway.com/deploy/flowengine--dark-cool
scoreRationale.feasibility: Parsing is easy, but rewiring nodes to a Data Table reliably across versions is fiddly: https://community.n8n.io/t/what-is-your-trick-for-handing-over-n8n-workflows-without-the-credentials-setup-pain/323533
scoreRationale.complianceBurden: Re-scoped to browser-only processing with no stored API keys, though exports can hold secrets in node parameters: https://community.n8n.io/t/how-do-you-hand-over-n8n-workflows-to-clients-heres-the-format-im-working-on/322030

review.findings: The reviewer found the evidence less independent than it looked: AntoBel4 is validating FlowDossier, easybits sells templates, and only Katie_LoopsFTW is a clearly independent buyer. All confirmed prices are one-off ($9-19), undercutting a monthly plan, and FlowEngine (free, open source) already gives clients a portal, so the live-page angle was dropped. The one real gap is a client-safe edit surface, because n8n's restrictive roles need Cloud Pro or Enterprise; the original design's stored client API keys were rated a security burden, so the idea was re-scoped to a browser-only generator of an importable form plus Data Table add-on and an acceptance test, sold per handover. Reviewer scores pain 3, WTP 2, reachability 4, competitiveGap 2, feasibility 3, complianceBurden 2; complianceBurden was raised to 3 after the re-scope removed stored keys.

missing: willingnessToPay 2 is below 3: no payment found for client-safe editing
only one clearly independent complaint; the others are from builders validating their own products
gateGap.closedBy: The by-hand packs for 5 freelancers close the largest gap (willingness to pay): 2 paid second packs would move WTP to 3 and supply independent complaints, lifting the total to about 19 to 20; validation would still need a second independent buyer complaint.

runNotes.caveats: Only one idea ships, against a first-run target of 3. Six candidates were reviewed and five were killed outright, each because a free or very cheap product already does the job (Flowlert, Lovable's built-in scan, PixelGuard's free plan, free PHP 8.4 scanners); the developer-tooling lens on small-business automation and Shopify surfaced markets crowded with indie tools launched in 2026, and many forum 'complaints' were market-validation posts by those builders. Theme Conflict Merge ships as provisional at 17 although its reviewer recommended a kill: the reviewer's own findings left one gap (Shopify's updater drops every edit when any file conflicts, and the $9/month incumbent does not list Horizon), and the idea was re-scoped to that case. Because one idea ships, the complexity-mix constraint (a Weekend MVP plus a Multi-week) is not met. Watchlist re-research (Canvas maintenance, ADA demand letters, agent exposure audit) found no new payment evidence. A3's GitHub path returned 422 only because queries lacked is:issue; with it the API works. The OOTS evidence date (2025-02-15) is older than 180 days; the freelancer job date comes from the API's time_submitted. Extra run (random sources A11 A2 B1 C7 C1): added ideas 2, 3 and 4 (Accessibility Fleet Log, Health Page Tracker Watch, Client Safe-Edit Pack for n8n), all provisional after review. The random sources leaned to education and yielded little; two of the three ideas came from A11 (WordPress accessibility plugin reviews) and the third is a re-scoped watchlist entry. Seven candidates were reviewed: three watchlist entries were killed (Canvas content maintenance, ADA demand-letter ledger, Agent Exposure Audit), and four were rescored, of which Horizon regression check (18) was held back because it shares idea 1's customer. Health Page Tracker Watch overlaps in mechanism with Consent Leak Watch (2026-11-02) but targets health practices and BAA/consumer-health-data exposure, not consent banners. Pricing-page evidence items are undated; their date is the date read. The n8n pack's complianceBurden was raised from the reviewer's 2 to 3 because the re-scope removed stored API keys. Extra run (random sources A6 A5 B9 C6 C5): added no ideas. The day already held 4 provisional ideas, the maximum ROUTINE.md and the validator allow, so only a validated idea could have shipped. No candidate came near the gate: the best two (Text Consent Ledger 18 and Oversell Watch 16) were rescored to 14 by reviewers. The FCC revocation rule (2026-21821, effective 2026-11-25) is real mandate evidence for any future small-business texting idea. The watchlist is unchanged.
